Findings at a glance

KS2 can modestly beat the unchanged MLP in this harness, but the gains depend on the training pool and geometry basis. Learned projections, ReLU² output features and smaller spine charts close the earlier demuxed-history architecture's loss gap. The table compares two useful rank-1 candidates after 100,000 updates. Negative gaps favor KS2; losses are nats per byte. Every model has four FFNs. The original MLP has 73,728 learned parameters per FFN (294,912 across four); uniform rank-1 KS2 has 73,600 per FFN (294,400 across four).

Combining wins is conditional. None of the eleven new combinations beats the same-extension uniform rank-1 mean at 15k. At 100k, rank-1 plus the power basis improves all three original-pool seeds over both MLP and the earlier rank-1 parent on exploratory validation. On the larger pool, all four combinations trail the earlier Hermite-basis rank-1 mean. The reserved comparisons above provide a separate confirmation check; they were not used to choose configurations. Same-architecture repeat variation and only three seeds limit claims about small differences.

The requested MLP subspace gives no clear incremental gain. The mixed cell includes two rank-16 charts in every FFN. Replacing 32 rank-1 features with a separate ReLU² MLP branch leaves 368 projected features and uses 72,916 learned parameters per FFN versus 73,172 for its mixed KS2-only parent. The exploratory mean change is −0.000217; on fresh reserved text it is +0.000122 (1/3 seed wins). The mixed variants do not improve the uniform rank-1 exploratory mean. These are 15k tests of spine-only KS2; they do not isolate the benefit of rank-16 charts or test mixed-rank full edge/damping cells.

Efficiency is measured separately from loss. The following are median whole-step times from five randomized rounds on one MI100, B4 × 64 bytes, FP32. The MLP branch uses the same input/readout projections as the KS2 coordinates.

ModelMilliseconds per training step
Original MLP7.474
Uniform rank-1 KS28.122
Uniform rank-1 KS2, power basis8.133
Mixed KS2 ranks9.006
Mixed KS2 + MLP subspace9.115

Fused geometry reduces cost, while shared RWKV blocks dominate the isolated block timings. This identifies a compute target, not an attention-capacity explanation for loss. Compact Hadamard storage is about 12× smaller but its tested training step is 2.45× slower. Rank-1 provides more independent scalar geometry inputs; scale-only interventions do not explain its advantage. Rank grouping, warp count and basis conditioning remain partly confounded.

428 completed training runs; 259 fresh reserved evaluations. The study uses the original MLP as its sole primary control. All final training starts preceded the two-hour extension's cutoff; in-flight runs then finished. Detailed comparisons, prior RHAC/RWKV evidence, numerical checks and all outcomes follow. No claim of a universal KS2 advantage is warranted.

Protocol and interpretation

The exploration starts at 2026-10-22 23:22:13 UTC. The original four-hour window ended at 03:22:13 UTC; the user explicitly extended work by another four hours, through 2026-10-23 07:22:13 UTC. New training jobs stop launching at the deadline; already running jobs finish. Final scoring, auditing and reporting follow. Four AMD MI100 GPUs run independent experiments concurrently, one model per GPU. This is not tensor parallelism.

Unless explicitly labeled otherwise, models have four layers, a 96-dimensional main stream, a 256-byte vocabulary, learned embeddings and an untied logit head. Training uses FP32, captured HIP graphs, AdamW, global gradient clipping at 1, weight decay 0.01 and a cosine learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0002. Batch size is 4 and sequence length is 64: 256 target bytes per update, 3.84 million targets in a 15,000-step screen and 25.6 million in a 100,000-step run. Sequence length 64 means 64 bytes here, not 64 source GPT-2 tokens.

Original training data: 4,468,985 decoded bytes from the first million source tokens. The larger training pool has 44,766,641 bytes from the first ten million tokens and contains the original pool as an exact prefix. Validation uses a separate 444,316-byte shard. Full-shard scoring averages four overlapping 64-byte tilings (offsets 0, 16, 32, 48), totaling 1,777,024 scored target visits. These are overlapping visits, not 1.78 million independent examples.

A second, disjoint 451,714-byte validation interval was reserved before final model comparison. After partial final scoring, the user requested a further two-hour combination study. That phase reserves a fresh 437,621-byte interval, documented below, and retains the earlier partial scores as diagnostics. No architecture tuning uses either reserved interval's scores. All exploratory validation comparisons remain subject to adaptive selection. Three seeds give useful replication, not a precise population confidence interval; tables show sample standard deviation, not standard error.

Initialization and sampling are paired within comparisons where shapes permit. Changing architecture changes random-number consumption and the optimization path; equal seed does not make every tensor identical. Shared attention, embedding and head initialization is checked explicitly. Warmup and timing updates are reset before training. Source snapshots, data hashes, commands, optimizer counters and restored-checkpoint evaluation accompany each run.

The earliest 20 runs recorded source hashes without per-run source copies. Their snapshots were subsequently recovered only after verifying exact equality with those recorded hashes; the recovery ledger is recovered_source_snapshots.json. Later workers snapshot sources directly. The final artifact audit checks source hashes, checkpoint steps, finite tensors and optimizer counters.

Fresh 100,000-step runs use a cosine schedule over the full 100,000 steps. Their 15k/50k intermediate checkpoints therefore do not match independently annealed 15k runs. Earlier 105k experiments used a different schedule: a 15k cosine followed by constant 0.0002. Historical results provide context, not a controlled head-to-head with this session.

Two-hour extension to combine improvements

The user requested a new two-hour window specifically to combine successful KS2 changes: 2026-10-23 15:21:56 UTC through 2026-10-23 17:21:56 UTC. The previous 359 training runs had already completed. The original MLP remains fixed. The new screen has twelve KS2 configurations and three seeds each, followed by selected 100k replications on both training pools.

The earlier reserved scoring had already evaluated 109 checkpoints when this request arrived. Those outputs and 34 completed timing cases are preserved in the interrupted evaluation record, and are not used for combination selection. A fresh, disjoint interval at source validation tokens 2,000,000–2,099,999 is reserved for final confirmation. Its decoded size is 437,621 bytes. Old evaluation files remain unchanged, and new scores use separate filenames.

The screen combines small charts with power-basis optimization, slow geometry learning, warp-only or frozen geometry, and bias/gain calibration. Polynomial reparameterization combined with frozen coefficients is deliberately excluded as a new architecture: after coefficient conversion it describes the same fixed polynomial, so that combination would largely test floating-point implementation differences. Recorded plan · Structural, gradient and unchanged-control checks · Fresh interval provenance.

The additive prediction is loss(power) + loss(slow) − loss(parent), using the same seed and horizon. A negative residual means a better result than adding the individual observed effects; a positive residual means worse. A negative interaction can simply mean that two individually harmful changes do less harm together than their summed penalties: it does not establish that the combined model beats its parent. This small factorial contrast describes these training runs, not a statistical proof of synergy. Nonlinear optimization and floating-point trajectory variation can produce interactions.

Architectures and the route information takes

Selected demuxed-history baseline

main[96] → LayerNorm → RWKV-7 → add to main
                                  ↓ post-attention main[96]
    concat(post-attention main, side[2048], prior post-attention and post-decoder main states)
      → normalization / causal time mixing → fixed Hadamard mux → 64 × 8 coordinates
      → coordinates + KS2 geometry → fixed Hadamard demux → learned output gains
      → add to (main[96], side[2048])
    keep post-attention and post-decoder main states as next layers' history
    final main[96] → normalization → learned logits[256]

The side residual bypasses attention, embeddings and logits; it is a decoder-to-decoder state. Decoder inputs have widths 2144, 2336, 2528 and 2720. Attention continues to receive a direct 96D residual state. Only decoder updates are demuxed into that state. The final side output does not reach the task loss; its 2048 output gains are counted in the parameter budget even though they receive no task gradient.

Learned-projection KS2

main → RWKV residual update
         → normalization / causal FFN time mixing
         → learned 96-to-(charts × 8) input projection
         → coordinates + KS2 geometry
         → optional feature activation (usually ReLU²)
         → learned (charts × 8)-to-96 output projection → residual add

The canonical full model has 31 rank-8 charts and 613,168 learned parameters. Undamped KS2 removes the denominator calculation and uses 33 charts at 615,120 parameters. Spine-only KS2 retains the spine and its two warps, removes edge terms, and uses 46 charts at 612,848 parameters. The original MLP uses learned projections and ReLU² at width 384, totaling 615,936 parameters. An archived width-368 diagnostic has 603,648; it is not the primary control.

These learned-projection variants intentionally change the selected baseline's decoder routing and omit its 2048D side/history path. They isolate whether the KS2 cell can work with conventional adaptive routing. Their improvements cannot all be attributed to a single projection change in the original baseline.

The original MLP input weights initialize uniformly within ±0.5/√width; the KS2 projection uses ±1/√width. The alternate MLP diagnostics match the latter range. Output projections start at zero, as in the original residual architecture.

Rank-1 spine candidate used in the combination study

normalized / time-mixed main[96]
      → learned projection → 368 scalar coordinates c
      → each coordinate gets its own spine g(c): six coefficients + two warp parameters
      → ReLU(c + g(c))²
      → learned projection → residual update[96]

For each scalar chart, the basis argument is 4 tanh(c/4). The implementation also clamps coordinates to the FP16 finite range while evaluating geometry in FP32. This candidate keeps the KS2 spine but omits the full cell's edge and damping terms. It acts as a bank of learned scalar nonlinearities between two learned projections, rather than using cross-coordinate geometry within each chart. All 96 main-stream inputs can influence every scalar through the learned projection. The two projections cost 70,656 parameters per FFN, and the 368 × 8 spine parameters add 2,944, for 73,600 total. Freezing those 2,944 coefficients retains their nonlinear function; learned bias calibration adds 368 parameters before the ReLU² transform.

Mixed KS2 ranks and an MLP branch

During the two-hour extension, the user requested mixed KS2 ranks, two rank-16 charts, and an MLP in its own subspace. These are mixtures within every FFN, not different ranks assigned to different layers. Each of the four FFNs keeps one learned 96→368 input projection and one learned 368→96 output projection. Disjoint coordinate groups use their own KS2 spine charts; every projected coordinate can depend on all 96 main-stream inputs.

The hybrid replaces 32 rank-1 coordinates in the balanced mixture with a 32-feature ReLU² MLP branch. Its hidden coordinates receive no KS2 geometry. The branch outputs concatenate with the KS2 outputs before the shared learned readout. Equivalently, the MLP branch has a learned 96→32 input projection and a learned 32→96 output contribution. It does not increase the 368-feature allocation or add a separate residual path.

What the mixed-rank experiment suggests

Among the all-KS2 spine variants, the mean ordering is uniform rank-1 (368 independent spine summaries), rank-1-heavy mixture (258), then balanced mixture (154). This is consistent with the hypothesis that more independently evaluated scalar geometry is useful at this small decoder width. It does not isolate summary count: chart grouping, mean-input scale and the number of learned warp parameters change together. The earlier scale-only interventions did not reproduce the rank benefit.

The hybrid has 122 KS2 summaries plus 32 ordinary ReLU² features and performs close to the balanced all-KS2 mixture. Its small mean gain does not show that MLP and KS2 provide strongly complementary features. Every model still has 368 raw coordinate bypasses and 368 output activations, so the count of spine summaries is not a rank bound on the complete FFN. Two rank-16 charts are present in every requested mixture, but the experiment does not establish that rank-16 charts help: there is no otherwise-identical mixture without them. These are findings about the tested spine-only cell, not a test of mixed-rank full edge/damping geometry.

Scheduling the late mixed-rank request

The end-of-queue forecast could not start every new three-seed test before the cutoff. The long-run dispatcher and its four active workers were therefore suspended in memory while the short mixed-rank screen uses the four GPUs. No checkpoint was reloaded, no optimizer state was reset and no training steps were removed. All workers had resumed by 15.25 minutes after suspension.

The suspended runs' raw elapsed training times can include the suspension and are excluded from speed comparisons. Their original measurements remain in the raw artifacts, with suspension flags in the flat ledger. Controlled final timing uses separate fresh processes and is unaffected. Exact process identities and suspension/resumption timestamps · Scheduling forecast.

Counts sum all four layers. For a dense rank-8 KS2 chart at model width 96, the two projections cost 1,536 parameters. Full geometry adds 820, undamped geometry 692, and spine geometry 50. With four FFNs, the dense family has 321,024 common parameters plus four times the chart count times its per-chart cost.

Full geometry uses about 35% of the dense 31-chart decoder budget; spine geometry uses about 3% of the 46-chart budget. Thus the matched-total-budget spine configuration also has 368 projected features instead of 248. Its gain over the full cell cannot be attributed solely to the removed terms. Learned-versus-frozen spine preserves the 368-feature width and initialized tensors, providing a direct KS2 comparison of geometry training. Frozen geometry retains 9,200 fixed values even though they no longer count as learned parameters. Frozen rank-4 spine retains 9,568 fixed geometry values; frozen full geometry at 46 charts retains 150,880. The latter has 754,528 learned plus fixed coefficients and therefore exceeds the original MLP's total coefficient storage despite its lower learned parameter count. Power-basis spine has the same counts as learned rank-8 spine; its coefficient coordinates change, not its function-class dimension.

The long runs test a complete training regime; they do not isolate horizon from schedule.

KS2 basis conditioning and chart rank

The power and Taylor bases are invertible reparameterizations of the original four Hermite terms. Coefficients are transformed so the initial mathematical function is preserved; the optimizer now acts in different coordinates. The two warped Chebyshev terms remain. This tests optimization conditioning without claiming a larger function class. Independent CPU checks compare geometry values, coordinate gradients, and complete nonzero-readout model logits.

Rank 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 spine variants retain 368 projected features and identical input projection tensors. Regrouping changes the shared scalar mean supplied to each spine and slightly changes warp parameter count. Rank 1 tests whether cross-coordinate coupling itself helps; it still retains KS2 geometry. In the spine-only cell, every output within a chart evaluates its basis at the same scalar mean of that chart: G_j(c) = sum_m a_mj phi_m(mean(c)). At 368 projected features, rank 8 supplies 46 distinct scalar means, whereas rank 1 supplies 368. The 6 coefficients per projected feature remain; rank 1 adds per-chart warp parameters. Thus this comparison changes the diversity of the geometry inputs as well as coordinate grouping. The coordinate ReLU² path still has 368 features in either case, and each learned input projection can mix all 96 model dimensions. A rank-1 advantage would support independent learned scalar geometry in this harness, not establish that richer cross-coordinate geometry never helps. Full-geometry rank 2 and 4 variants instead reallocate the total parameter budget between feature width and quadratic-cost edges. Geometry-only RMS normalization preserves the raw coordinate bypass. Parallel and after-activation placements test whether applying ReLU² after geometry is the limiting interaction. Every model stays within the original 615,936 parameter budget.

Why chart rank changes the spine pathway

The spine-only geometry computes one scalar summary per chart: t = 4 tanh(mean(c) / 4), then each chart output is G_j(c) = Σ_m a_mj φ_m(t). The six basis responses depend on the same scalar t. Away from nondifferentiable boundaries, the geometry Jacobian has the outer-product form J_G = (dG/dt) (dt/dc), so it has rank at most one within each chart. This is an algebraic property of the implemented spine, not an empirical estimate of the whole model's information capacity.

At 368 projected features, rank-8 charts supply 46 independently evaluated scalar summaries; rank-4 charts supply 92; rank-1 charts supply 368. Each output retains its own six coefficients, but smaller charts give those coefficients more distinct scalar inputs. That is a plausible explanation for the replicated small-chart advantage. The experiment also changes the number of per-chart warp parameters, so it does not isolate scalar-summary count perfectly.

The decoder itself is not restricted to a rank-one Jacobian per chart: it carries the coordinate bypass c + G(c), followed by ReLU² and a learned output projection. Each learned input coordinate can mix all 96 model dimensions before chart grouping. Therefore, a rank-1 chart is a learned nonlinear function of a full-model projection, not a decision to ignore the other 95 model dimensions. Full geometry adds coordinate-dependent edges and damping, which do not obey the spine-only rank bound.

This separates two hypotheses. More independent scalar responses may be a better use of the small decoder budget; alternatively, smaller charts may be easier to optimize. The learned/frozen rank comparisons and the function-preserving basis experiments help distinguish these explanations, while the 100k runs test whether the short-horizon ordering persists.

Chart rank also changes basis scale and conditioning

On the same 1,024 training targets, all five learned-rank variants start with the same projected-coordinate RMS, about 0.513. Averaging within charts reduces the scalar supplied to the basis: its RMS is 0.505 at rank 1, 0.359 at rank 2, 0.256 at rank 4, 0.181 at rank 8 and 0.126 at rank 16. Thus chart grouping changes both the number of distinct scalar summaries and their initial scale.

The sampled basis-design condition number is about 103 at rank 1 versus 7,900 at rank 8 at initialization. At 15k updates, basis-input RMS is much closer (0.796 versus 0.771), but the corresponding condition summaries remain about 128 versus 2,024. Learned projections partly compensate for averaging, while the basis correlations and distribution of responses still differ. This supports conditioning as one plausible mechanism; it is not a causal decomposition of the observed loss advantage, and a design-matrix condition number is not the optimizer Hessian.

Original KS2 equation and bounded geometry inputs

Source review of RHAC identified a specific cell difference. Its local geometry uses the original mean and coordinate-sum weight decomposition, with softplus strengths multiplying absolute deviation and squared coordinate weights. The stabilized cell in this harness caps the spine, uses energy-normalized damping predicates, and bounds damping strengths. RHAC also feeds its geometry sigmoid(g/1.5). The following tests restore the original equation, apply sigmoid only to geometry inputs, and combine both. A fourth case adds the original positive-input geometry after the coordinate ReLU². Raw coordinate residuals and all projection tensors remain; each configuration has 613,168 learned parameters.

This is an adaptive follow-up motivated by source review, not a full RHAC reproduction. The primary MLP is unchanged. The local original equation was checked against the archived RHAC implementation for values and all gradients at positive, signed and zero-sum inputs. The four model factories preserve the original initialized tensors and zero-output function, pass nonzero-readout gradient and causality checks, and use eager geometry implementations. CPU checks.

Telemetry covers 1098 point samples from 2026-10-23T00:14:22.713362+00:00 through 2026-10-23T17:31:49.562520+00:00, approximately every 30 seconds. All four cards report at least 90% activity in 80.1% of those samples. Monitoring began after the study started; these are sampled activity readings, not a whole-study utilization integral or a measurement of peak FLOPs. Initialization, compilation and scoring transitions are included. See the summary and raw observations.

The final timing test interleaves the recorded reference and KS2 configurations on the same physical GPU in five randomized-order rounds. Each fresh process measures 100 captured training updates after warmup/reset, including batch copies and learning-rate writes. It excludes compilation and evaluation. This controls GPU assignment better than comparing independent runs on cards with different clocks. Sustained whole-training times remain available in the run ledger.

Times drift downward across the five rounds for every configuration. Other GPUs concurrently score held-out models during part of this window; the cause of the drift is not isolated. Randomized within-round ordering and the reported ranges matter more than millisecond precision. Same-round timing ratios preserve the comparison: uniform rank-1 KS2 is about 9% slower than MLP, and the mixed MLP-branch prototype about 21% slower. These short captured-step measurements do not guarantee the same sustained throughput under another workload.

Full geometry fusion reduces an isolated 64-chart forward/backward benchmark from about 1.430 ms to 0.418 ms. Undamped geometry falls from 0.685 to 0.168 ms, and spine-only from 0.270 to 0.073 ms. These are isolated kernels; total model speedups are smaller because attention, projections, optimizer and memory operations remain.

Validation covers random and extreme coordinates, masked tail sizes, zero initialization, all geometry gradients, captured execution and trained model parameters. At shared trained parameters, full-model maximum logit error was 1.57×10⁻⁵ and maximum parameter-gradient relative L2 error 3.26×10⁻⁶. Partial kernels have similarly small errors. They are numerically close, not bit-identical. Full training trajectories can diverge by several thousandths of loss.

One initial partial-kernel benchmark crashed because the checker reused a retained autograd graph across streams; using fresh copied cells fixed the harness. An earlier tanh approximation was replaced with the precise device tanh. The original full and partial kernels passed their checks; generalized-rank kernels are reported separately. These engineering failures and corrections are retained in the logs, not hidden as training failures.

Learned parameter count omits material storage. The history baseline has 2,270,208 bytes of FP32 learned weights but 37,489,664 bytes of fixed buffers for its stored projection codes. The original MLP has 2,463,744 weight bytes and no such buffers; canonical dense KS2 has 2,452,672 weight bytes and 1,488 buffer bytes. These figures describe the original dense-matrix code representation. The extended study below implements and evaluates compact blockwise Hadamard codes separately. Optimizer and activation memory are additional; per-run peak allocation is in the CSV/JSON.

There is a compute distinction as well. Summing input/output matrix sizes across four FFNs gives 9,371,648 projection multiply-accumulates per target for the history model, 190,464 for dense 31-chart KS2, and 294,912 for the original MLP. These counts exclude geometry, attention, normalization and backward. The fixed-code history implementation therefore performs about 49 times the projection work of dense 31-chart KS2 despite having fewer learned parameters. Its muxes are dense matrix operations, not implicit fast Hadamard transforms. Parameter compression alone does not deliver the corresponding compute or storage saving in this implementation.

Frozen geometry saves learned parameters and optimizer state, but retains its fixed geometry values and computation. Parameter-saving claims for frozen variants should therefore be read alongside storage and timing, not as free removal.

Prune the final unused side output

The final history decoder's 2048D side update has no consumer. An optional KS2 implementation keeps every decoder input and all geometry, but projects only the final 96D main update. On the trained 100k history checkpoint, CPU logits are identical and the maximum surviving-gradient absolute difference is 2.98×10⁻⁸. This removes 2,048 unused learned gains and 4,194,304 fixed-buffer bytes: 565,504 learned parameters and 33,295,360 buffer bytes remain. It also removes 1,048,576 forward projection MACs per target. These are functional-equivalence checks and an implementation optimization, not a new loss-improvement claim. The archived training runs and primary baseline remain unchanged. See the trained CPU check and GPU check.

Same-GPU median step time is 11.622 ms before pruning and 11.493 ms after pruning (1.1% lower). The five raw measurements per case are retained; this short benchmark is distinct from sustained training time.

Compact implementation of the original Hadamard codes

The original fixed codes can be represented by per-chart permutations, inverse permutations and post-Hadamard signs. Indices fit in signed 16-bit storage; signs use 8 bits. Identical code tables are shared across decoder layers and projections. FP32 blockwise Walsh transforms and folding implement the same linear map, with a different floating-point reduction order. All learned parameters remain unchanged.

For the trained 100k demuxed-history model, fixed-buffer storage drops from 37,489,664 to 3,116,032 bytes. CPU validation logits differ by at most 2.86e-05; loss differs by 1.19e-07. Individual projection and transpose derivatives are independently checked across 96/2144/2336/2528/2720 input widths.

Trained GPU check: PASS, max logit error 3.81e-05. All parameter-gradient relative errors are retained in the linked artifact.

Generalized geometry kernels and frozen-parameter savings

Equivalent fused geometry kernels cover ranks 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 in Hermite, power and Taylor coordinates. The GPU checker passed 450 forward/gradient cases, including extreme coordinates and fully learned, warp-only and frozen geometry. Trained model comparisons and captured optimizer updates also passed. The artifact records the exact kernel source hash used to gate subsequent training.

Frozen geometry still needs derivatives with respect to its inputs so the learned projections can train. The optimized backward pass keeps these derivatives while omitting unused geometry-parameter gradients. Warp-only training computes the warp derivatives but skips coefficient and damping-parameter reductions. These are implementation changes, not changes to the model function or learned parameter budget.

The initial strict elementwise check flagged three adversarial cases: two input gradients near zero coordinates and one forward result after large mixed-sign coordinates were clamped. Saved tensors were compared with independent CPU float64 autograd. Tiny-input gradient relative L2 errors were about 2×10⁻⁷ for the fused implementation; the clamp-stress forward error was 1.97×10⁻⁵. The eager reference also showed rounding error. Kernel code was unchanged. Ordinary-input and parameter-gradient tolerances remain strict; only these stress categories can use float64 checks, with relative L2 bounds of 10⁻⁵ for tiny input gradients and 5×10⁻⁵ for clamp forward outputs. Trained-model tolerances were unchanged.

Compute limits after simplifying KS2

For the frozen-spine model, the four isolated RWKV forward/backward modules total 4.753 ms, compared with 0.527 ms for its four complete FFNs. This shows a substantial common compute cost once the decoder is cheap. It does not establish that attention capacity causes the loss gap. Further KS2 kernel savings can have limited whole-step impact when attention, optimizer and other operations remain unchanged.

Quadratic features are a useful intervention. ReLU² and an unrectified square both reach about 1.624 in the full KS2 decoder, whereas ReLU and SiLU are about 1.642. This points toward feature magnitude/order rather than rectification alone. It does not show a KS2-specific advantage: pure square and ReLU² MLP controls are also included.

Projection learning rate does not transfer automatically. The original history scalar gains use an LR multiplier of 5.5. Carrying that multiplier into a dense learned output projection worsens loss to about 1.653. Geometry LR ×4 helps a plain KS2 cell, but stacking it with ReLU² worsens the stronger cell; larger multipliers are worse. LR multipliers adjust weight decay inversely so the per-step decay amount is held fixed.

Output factorization interacts with activation. In the history model, replacing gain-times-matrix main readout with a direct matrix helps ReLU² cases substantially, but does not rescue the plain KS2 cell by itself. A history model with random ReLU² features and a learned main readout also reaches about 1.624. Recovering adaptive readout is useful, but that benefit is not unique to learned KS2 geometry.

The factorized output also changes optimization: in y = gain × (Wf), a zero initial gain makes the initial gradient of a trainable W zero. A directly parameterized, zero-initialized W receives its readout gradient immediately. This is a mechanism implied by the parameterization, not a separate proof that it explains the entire observed loss difference. The strong random-feature/readout result also means these experiments do not establish that every input mux must become learned; adaptive output routing can recover much of the gap while retaining a fixed input mix.

Cheap learned rotations, mux affine transforms, coordinate RMS normalization, changing coordinate scale, removing the bypass and broad geometry-LR sweeps all appear in the full ledger. Most do not close the gap. Moving more of the fixed total budget into width-128 attention yields about 1.642 for both KS2 and MLP, worse than the width-96 allocation.

Is geometry inactive or wasted?

It is not inactive. In the trained history baseline, coordinate RMS grows from roughly 0.80 to 1.06 across layers, while geometry-update RMS grows from 0.60 to 1.17. Edge terms contribute more than spine terms in this trained model. Removing geometry after training raises sampled loss; removing the coordinate bypass can hurt even more. These are interventions on a trained solution, not comparisons to retrained alternatives.

In the learned-projection ReLU² model, geometry changes the sign of about 12–16% of coordinates before ReLU² and changes the positive feature vector by a relative norm of roughly 0.28–0.41. Zeroing all geometry increases the probe loss from about 1.699 to 1.833. The model relies on geometry even if a separately trained wider MLP can do better.

The damping contribution is weak, around 0.024 in the original trained history probe. Removing it at 31 charts preserves short-run quality while saving 15,872 parameters. Reinvesting that budget in 33 charts is therefore a sensible candidate. The full geometry has 820 parameters per chart, undamped geometry 692, and spine-only geometry 50.

The spine-only model allocates almost all its decoder budget to a wide learned projection, so its improvement over the full cell may partly come from width. Within KS2, freezing spine geometry preserves the 368-feature projection and initialized tensors: its three-seed short-run mean is 1.617121 versus 1.620510 for learned spine. The long-run comparison tests whether that advantage survives the longer schedule. Geometry dependence alone does not settle parameter efficiency.

Probes are stored beside the relevant runs as mechanism_probe.json and geometry_terms_probe.json. Probe losses use a smaller sample and must not be compared numerically with full-shard tables.

Each cell contains layers 1–4 in order. This CPU probe uses 1,024 fixed targets from the exploratory validation shard. It also records initialization, 15k and 50k checkpoints in the trajectory artifact. It does not inspect the reserved validation interval.

On the original-pool seed-11 runs, learned spine and undamped geometry become predominantly negative before the ReLU² transform. For learned spine, only about 2% of geometry entries are positive at 100k; geometry reduces the positive-coordinate fraction from about 20–32% to 10–17%, depending on layer. Frozen spine has roughly balanced geometry signs and barely changes that fraction; its learned input projection supplies much of the sparsity instead.

This suggests a concrete role for learned KS2 in these solutions: input-dependent thresholding before quadratic features. Geometry includes both a substantial average offset and sample-dependent variation, so it is not merely a constant bias. The observation motivates KS2-specific tests of threshold initialization and learning, but does not show that a simpler bias would reproduce the result.

Widespread saturation of the spine warp is not evident here. Its absolute tanh output exceeds 0.95 on fewer than 0.2% of sampled entries in every layer of the learned-spine 100k checkpoint. The average learned warp scale decreases from 1.137 at initialization to about 0.87–0.89. Geometry remains active: its RMS is about 0.76–1.45 times coordinate RMS, and its relative change to the positive quadratic feature vector is about 0.30–0.44. These are descriptive single-seed measurements, not proof that the same mechanism governs every configuration.

On 2,048 fixed exploratory validation targets, inference perturbations remove geometry, replace it with its training-calibrated mean, or subtract that mean. Constants are calibrated on a separate 2,048 training targets. No weights are retrained and no reserved validation is used. Positive deltas mean worse loss. Equivalent-basis conditioning probe

Design-matrix singular values were measured on 1,024 fixed training targets, using exactly the same sampled coordinates and warps for all bases. The first four Hermite terms span the same cubic polynomial space as powers or Taylor-scaled powers; coefficients are transformed before training so the initial function is unchanged. Power coordinates reduce the observed design condition number substantially in these checkpoints. This is a property of the sampled basis, not a measurement of the full optimizer Hessian and not proof of better generalization.

Replicated dependence on spine and edge terms

Across three independently trained full-geometry KS2 models, edge and spine outputs have comparable RMS amplitude. Removing either contribution from any individual layer increases loss on the same 4,096 exploratory validation targets. The edge geometry is therefore used by these trained models. Its parameter cost may still be less effective than allocating more projected features; inference dependence and the best retrained parameter allocation are different questions.

Freezing geometry removes its entries from the global gradient norm as well as preventing its updates. This CPU diagnostic measures that possible coupling on eight fixed training minibatches, with no optimizer steps. At the tested seed-11 endpoints, learned geometry contributes about 1.6–3.4% of squared gradient norm. Excluding it from the clipping norm changes the mean clip factor by roughly 0.006–0.013 in absolute terms.

These observations do not support geometry dominating global clipping at these checkpoints. They do not rule out different behavior earlier in training. AdamW normalizes using its moment estimates, so clipping factors are not direct learning-rate multipliers or measured parameter-update changes. See per-batch measurements and protocol.

Freezing spine geometry improved the replicated short-run result relative to learning it at the original rate. These KS2-only follow-ups isolate two explanations: geometry may need slower optimization, or one parameter family may be useful to adapt while another is better held fixed. All variants start from exactly the same geometry values as the learned-spine model; only trainability or its learning rate changes.

There are 46 rank-8 charts in each FFN. Warps-only training retains 368 learned geometry parameters across four layers, while coefficient-only training retains 8,832. Fixed geometry tensors still consume storage and computation. The original unchanged MLP and already completed learned/frozen spine runs are reused as references; no MLP variant is trained for this follow-up.

The earlier reference denoising KS2 used two geometry iterations; the language-model study initially used one. This follow-up applies the same learned geometry repeatedly before the output projection, with shared parameters: c ← c + αG(c). Every arm retains 31 rank-8 charts and 613,168 learned parameters. α=1 in the full two-step update, α=1/2 for two half steps, and α=1/4 for four quarter steps. ReLU², when present, is applied only after all iterations.

The reduced-step variants distinguish repeated nonlinear refinement from simply increasing the total update size. The plain two-step forward and all gradients match the reference stabilized cell exactly on CPU at nonzero output weights. GPU structural, finite-gradient and causal checks precede training. Repeated iterations cost more compute, so equal parameter count does not imply equal runtime.

This CPU probe uses the same 1,024 validation targets for each model and measures the vector entering the output projection. Participation rank is trace(C)²/trace(C²) for centered feature covariance. It is scale-dependent and measures variance concentration on this sample, not intrinsic information capacity.

There is no simple monotonic relationship between feature rank and validation quality. The plain learned-projection KS2 model has high feature rank in some layers yet worse loss than the quadratic variants. Some strong MLP and KS2 models have a low-rank, high-magnitude last or penultimate feature distribution. This does not support a blanket explanation that all poor KS2 results come from collapsed or unused coordinates. The raw statistics, entropy ranks and quantiles are in feature_probe.json.

How this compares with the earlier experiments

The earlier three-seed 15k MLP reference averaged 1.622722; the selected demuxed-history model averaged 1.666841. Fresh controls reproduce that broad gap. Increasing the decoder-only side residual to 2048 dimensions and increasing charts from 32 to 64 helped relative to smaller side streams, but did not by itself beat the MLP.

The single-mux architecture changed the information path: KS2 and RWKV branches ran in parallel, so KS2 no longer received the same-layer post-attention state. Static input/output gains only modestly helped. An extra KS2 modulation subspace, whose weighted output vectors were summed then RMS-normalized, improved that model to about 1.6758, still behind the demuxed-history reference at about 1.6669. Raw-history and attention-pass-through variants did not resolve the gap. The current evidence favors retaining useful routing while testing decoder changes separately.

Replacing every RWKV linear projection with fixed Hadamard muxes reduced learned parameters from 567,552 to 306,944 but raised loss from 1.665535 to 1.767811. Individual read/key/value/output replacements each hurt. Gate-up was the promising exception: 543,360 parameters and 1.665681. The new gate-budget experiments test that exception in a different decoder rather than assuming it is universally free.

The requested RWKV-8 comparison was performed using a local, similarly sized adaptation of BlinkDL's RWKV7+ROSA parallel hybrid, pinned at commit 20be0f8cf0bdf506d8c0030c87a9a3416f95b143. The parameter-matched adaptation scored 1.673763 at 567,296 parameters and 19.73 ms/step, versus baseline 1.666923 at 567,552 parameters and 15.64 ms/step. Keeping the original RWKV controller sizes plus ROSA scored 1.671107 at 619,520 parameters and 20.14 ms/step. Reducing controllers without ROSA scored 1.675211, so ROSA partially recovered that reduced model's loss but did not beat the original baseline.

This RWKV-8 result is specifically a 64-byte-context local adaptation. The official demonstration lacked a ROSA training backward; this implementation supplies exact single-bit counterfactual credits with a Bernoulli surrogate. Forward suffix matching and GPU credits were checked against references. It is not an official full-scale RWKV-8 training recipe, and it does not test long-context ROSA benefits. See the full RWKV-8 summary and the pinned upstream source.

Earlier 105k all-MLP runs averaged 1.540879; adding a tiny KS2 branch to the inner two MLP FFNs averaged 1.540212, a very small difference under that protocol. This is evidence of compatibility, not a demonstrated general lead. Earlier normal-attention nanoGPT tests also found near-equality (7.819336 MLP versus 7.823028 KS2), but used a full GPT-2 vocabulary, only 500 CPU updates and a different scale. Their token losses are not comparable to byte losses here.

The repository's controlled patch-denoising study does contain a substantial KS2 lead: the reference 433,452-parameter KS2 achieved 27.388 dB mean Set12 PSNR versus 26.303 dB for the 435,030-parameter MLP, with three seeds and 3,000 main updates. That task uses normalized image patches, squared-error loss, learned projections and two geometry iterations; its MLP uses tanh. This is meaningful evidence for KS2 on that task, not evidence that the same cell must beat a ReLU² residual language-model FFN. The compact stabilized denoising and quantized exports show additional storage/speed opportunities, but use different sizes and training procedures. See the recorded denoising protocol and results.

Relation to RHAC history conditioning

The RHAC source clarifies which parts of that architecture were transferred into this experiment. The Hadamard encoder is in rhac.py; the current postdown.py implements a separate signed-bucket residual conditioner. The language-model harness reuses the permutation, block-Hadamard and sign construction, then folds a full view into each rank-8 chart so every FFN input reaches every chart coordinate. RHAC's spread views retain their full width before routing.

AspectRHAC spread-conditioned graftDemuxed-history KS2 harness
Role of KS2Correction to intact pretrained SwiGLU activations; base projections stay frozenReplacement FFN learned from scratch; fixed input/output codes with learned output gains
HistoryDetached completed decoder states, collapsed to an RMS-matched depth meanDifferentiable concatenation of separate post-attention and post-FFN main states plus the side residual
Learned routingPretrained gate/up/down projections plus learned history landing vectorsFixed folded Hadamard input and transpose output directions; scalar output gains
Local coordinatessigmoid(g/1.5), original KS2 equation, normally two geometry iterationsRaw projected coordinates, stabilized KS2 equation, one iteration in the baseline
Correction placementAdded to SiLU(g), then multiplied by the intact up branchKS2 output demuxed into the residual stream

These differences explain why a successful compressed history conditioner does not by itself establish that fixed multiplexers can replace every learned FFN projection at the same quality. That is an inference about the architectural comparison, not a negative result for RHAC. The current study directly tests learned routing, geometry iteration, coordinate statistics and local equation choices; it does not reproduce the full pretrained RHAC adaptation protocol or infer its quality from source code.

What the evidence supports next

Carry forward both rank-1 basis choices as KS2 candidates. The power-basis combination beats the fixed MLP on all three fresh reserved seeds for both training pools, while the original Hermite-basis rank-1 variant retains the stronger larger-pool mean. The power basis improves the original-pool parent comparison but does not provide a universal additive improvement. Keep both results and their training-pool dependence visible. The mixed-rank MLP branch does not show a dependable incremental benefit: its tiny exploratory improvement reverses on fresh reserved text. Further work on that branch needs a specific mechanistic hypothesis, rather than treating this result as an established win.

Keep the original MLP reference fixed and spend further search on KS2. Match total parameters, training targets, optimizer updates and data when evaluating a KS2 improvement. Preserve the original MLP initialization, width and optimizer rather than moving the comparison target during the search.

Retain adaptive routing and quadratic features in further KS2 tests. Those variants deliver larger observed improvements than static mux gains or wider attention in this study, although the routing comparison also changes the side/history path. Fixed multiplexing can still be useful for parameter/storage tradeoffs, but equal exposure of every coordinate is not the same as learned task-specific routing.

Separate geometry expressivity from budget allocation. Removing damping reduces parameter and compute cost, but the replicated 100k undamped models underperform the unchanged MLP on both pools. The early single-seed result does not justify making that the default. Compare learned, slowed and selectively frozen geometry within KS2 while preserving its projection width and initialization. Judge geometry ablations after retraining as well as by inference-time lesion tests, and retain the original MLP as the external benchmark.

Isolate the number of spine inputs from warp parameter count. A targeted next experiment would compare the existing rank-8 spine with 368 scalar spines whose warp parameters are shared in groups of eight. That would preserve 368 feature coordinates, six coefficients per feature and the rank-8 warp budget, while changing whether outputs evaluate one shared mean or separate scalar inputs. A separate scale factor could then test the remaining input-scale confound. This experiment is proposed, not performed in this session.

Distinguish scalar spine improvements from full geometric interactions. The rank-1 and mixed-rank follow-ups retain the spine-only simplification. Their results do not establish that mixed-rank edge/damping geometry is ineffective. A future full-cell mixture would need its own matched-budget comparison, because higher ranks spend substantially more parameters on edge interactions. The present results support a useful KS2-derived FFN candidate; they do not validate every part of the original multiplexed architecture.

Carry the verified kernels forward, with trajectory replication. Fusion makes more comparisons feasible. Preserve the eager reference and all-gradient checks. Small single-seed loss leads are not convincing when repeats and floating-point paths move by similar amounts.

The remaining uncertainty is about scaling and task distribution: larger models, more distinct data, longer context, alternative KS2 rank/chart allocation and task-adapted coordinate statistics could change the ordering. This session tests several of those pressures at small scale; it does not establish that KS2 must win, nor that it cannot.

Widths are rounded upward, so the MLP receives slightly more total parameters (less than 0.2% extra). Unlike earlier inner-two-layer budget tests, this sweep directly tests all-decoder parameter allocation. Negative gaps favor KS2. All twelve completed seed/budget pairs favor MLP: the mean KS2 penalties are approximately 0.0066, 0.0051, 0.0087 and 0.0106 nats/byte. This is evidence against a small-budget advantage for this particular one-step full-geometry + ReLU² implementation under the tested training protocol.

The original MLP and FeatureCell-based matched MLP have the same mathematical FFN shape but use different initialization paths as well as different input scales. Their difference alone therefore cannot isolate scale. This additional control constructs the same 384-wide MLP twice from the same seed, then doubles only its input weights in one arm. Attention, embeddings, output weights and all random directions are identical; optimizer and training positions are paired.

This completed diagnostic tests input scale directly. It does not replace the original MLP reference, and no further MLP initialization search follows it. Its relevance to future work is that KS2 input scaling deserves controlled tests within KS2 itself.

The transfer uses causal softmax attention with three 32D heads and RoPE, pre-normalization, and no RWKV FFN time mixing. All compared FFNs receive the same attention implementation and paired attention initialization. These models have about 490–493k parameters, so their absolute losses should not be compared to 615k RWKV models as if only attention changed.

This test distinguishes a uniquely RWKV-specific failure from a decoder mismatch that persists under ordinary attention. The alternate MLP initialization changes results here too. At this short horizon the KS2 variants do not show a consistent broad lead.

The earlier Hadamard projection sweep identified RWKV gate-up as an apparently inexpensive place to remove learned weights. This session tests whether its saved 24,192 parameters can buy wider FFNs. The gate mux adds fixed-code storage as well. Historical near-equality on the original history model does not guarantee that it transfers to a different FFN.

The context study keeps training target count fixed at 3.84 million: batch 1 × length 256 for 15k updates, batch 16 × length 64 for 3,750 updates, and batch 4 × length 256 for 3,750 updates. It compares MLP384, spine46 and undamped33 at seed 11. The original batch 4 × length 64 × 15k runs serve as references.

Changing context length changes both usable history and the number of recurrent positions. Changing batch size at fixed targets changes the number of optimizer updates. These are separate factors; a single longer-context score cannot identify the cause. The table evaluates exactly the same 64 target bytes with 64 versus 256 input context, avoiding the different context-position mixture of ordinary full-window averages.

Most of the apparent longer-context gain comes from inference context, not longer-context training. On the same target positions with 256 input bytes, the MLP trained at length 64 scores 1.573303 and the MLP trained at length 256 scores 1.573143. Spine KS2 scores 1.575246 versus 1.576085; undamped KS2 scores 1.581946 versus 1.584891. Thus the longer training windows do not improve these seed-11 comparisons meaningfully at matched training targets. The 64-trained recurrent model already benefits from additional evaluation context. This supports keeping the faster 64-byte training setup for the main long-horizon comparison.

Batch 4 × length 256 for 3,750 updates gave spine KS2 a small initial lead over MLP. The table below adds two independent paired seeds. These scores use full 256-byte tilings, unlike the suffix-only table above; compare within each table. This completed diagnostic used an alternate MLP initialization and is not a primary-reference win. Reproduction and artifacts

Use /home/curved/int8-vllm/.venv/bin/python with the recorded ROCm environment. Wave manifests specify every configuration and seed. study_checked_v6.py validates model structure, gradients and causality before dispatch; versioned study_wave scripts run up to four independent workers. The first long runs use v8 and selective-geometry follow-ups use v9. Extended conditioning screens use v10, calibration screens use v12, and generalized-rank freezing uses v14. The original-equation tests and selected extended long runs use v15. The final geometry-input-scale follow-up uses v17, preserving v15 behavior when its optional scale is absent. Extended evaluations use v16/v17, including the documented batch-size handling for the original signed equation. The combination screens and long replications use v18, which installs bias/gain calibration after rank changes and freezing so the new calibration parameters remain trainable. The user-requested mixed-rank and MLP-branch follow-up uses v19, which delegates all earlier configurations unchanged to v18. Final reserved scoring uses the v19 evaluator and the fresh interval specified in final_holdout_plan.json. Earlier waves retain their versioned factories. The exact source used by each run is copied into its sources/ directory; using today's top-level files alone is not a substitute for checking those snapshots.

python study_collect.py --root gpu_runs/goal_20261022_232213
python study_plot.py --root gpu_runs/goal_20261022_232213
python study_report_figures.py --root gpu_runs/goal_20261022_232213
python study_extended_figures.py --root gpu_runs/goal_20261022_232213
python study_report.py --root gpu_runs/goal_20261022_232213

The actual interpreter and repository-relative paths are in each run's command.json. study_final_checks_v19.py specifies the final reserved holdout and randomized same-GPU speed protocol. gpu_telemetry.jsonl records utilization and clocks. prior_snapshots/ and prior_additional/ preserve historical summaries used for comparison. Figures are standalone SVG and PNG. original_reference_check.json verifies that the restored primary MLP has exactly the original initialized tensors and optimizer hyperparameters for all three seeds. control_correction.json records canceled alternate-control work.

Download source bundle · Bundle verification and coverage. The archive indexes the exact source versions for each completed run by SHA256, alongside separately labeled current analysis tools and manifests. It excludes datasets and trained weights. Regenerate with study_source_bundle.py --root gpu_runs/goal_20261022_232213 after the last run so its coverage includes the complete study.

Goal completion review records the requirements, evidence and any checks still pending. Artifact generation alone does not establish that all research and reporting requirements are finished.
